posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the bait shop)
posts.quote: THE BAIT SHOP KEPT THE NIGHT CRAWLERS IN THE SAME REFRIGERATOR AS THE LUNCH MEAT, AND NOBODY EVER COMPLAINED.
posts.caption: The bait shop opened before the sun did, and the first thing you noticed was the hum of the cooler. Inside, the night crawlers lived in paper cartons on the same shelf as the sandwich meat and the bottles of orange pop. The owner sold you a dozen crawlers, a pack of hooks, and a bologna sandwich in a single trip to the register. He wrapped everything in the same newspaper and never once mixed them up. Nobody wanted to ask how he kept it straight. By the time you were sitting at the end of the dock with a thermos, it hardly mattered anyway.
posts.first: My uncle bought his bait there every April, and he bought his lunch meat in the very same stop. He swore the sandwiches tasted better after sitting beside the worms, which I never believed for a second. He still ate every one of them.

posts.quote: THE TUBE TESTER AT THE DRUGSTORE DOOR LET DAD CHECK HIS OWN RADIO, AND HE NEVER WALKED PAST IT.
posts.caption: Near the front door of the drugstore stood a tall metal cabinet with a glass dial and rows of little sockets. Dad would carry the glowing tubes out of the back of our radio in a paper sack, then stand there plugging them in one at a time. The needle swung to GOOD or to BAD, and he nodded like a doctor reading an X-ray. If a tube had gone bad, he bought a new one right there off the shelf, and the radio was working again by supper. Nobody called a repairman for something a person could fix with a paper sack and ten minutes. It was the closest thing Dad had to a hobby that came with an answer.
posts.first: Dad kept a cigar box of spare tubes in the basement, each one wrapped in tissue. When the radio went quiet on a Sunday afternoon, he was down the stairs before anyone asked. I can still hear the click of that box when he put it away.

posts.quote: Every town had one clock that was never right, and everybody used it anyway.
posts.first: The one on our courthouse ran four minutes fast, and my grandfather set his watch by it every morning on purpose. He said it gave him a head start. He was never late a day in his life.

posts.quote: GRANDPA BROUGHT A TRANSISTOR RADIO TO THE BALLGAME, SO HE HEARD EVERY PLAY TWICE.
posts.caption: Grandpa never trusted his own eyes at a ballgame. He bought his ticket, climbed to the same row in the bleachers, and then pressed a small plastic transistor radio to his ear. The announcer told him what he was watching a half second after he watched it, and Grandpa nodded along as if the two of them were comparing notes. If a play went by too quickly, the radio caught it for him. Every few innings he leaned over and gave us the score, though the scoreboard stood right in front of us. We learned to say thanks, Grandpa, and keep eating our peanuts.
posts.first: He carried that radio in his shirt pocket and wore out three sets of batteries every summer. The static between stations was part of the game for me. When I hear a crowd roar on a tiny speaker, I still think of his hand cupped over his ear.

posts.quote: THE FIELD TRIP / A SIGNED SLIP, A BAG LUNCH, AND A WINDOW SEAT ON THE BUS
posts.caption: The permission slip came home folded in quarters at the bottom of your book bag. It needed a signature and sometimes fifty cents, and it needed both before Friday. On the morning of the trip you carried a lunch in a brown paper bag with your name on it and a jelly sandwich squashed flat from the ride. The bus smelled like warm vinyl and somebody's grape soda. You fought for the window seat, and the teacher counted heads every time the doors opened. Nobody remembers what the trip was actually for, only who sat with whom.
posts.first: I once lost my permission slip in a puddle, and my mother wrote a new one on the back of a grocery receipt. The teacher accepted it without a word. I sat by the window that day and felt like I had won something.

posts.quote: THE CORNER GROCER KEPT EVERY FAMILY'S TAB IN A LITTLE BLACK BOOK, AND NOBODY EVER ASKED TO SEE IT.
posts.caption: Every family on our street had a page in the corner grocer's little black notebook. You picked up your flour and coffee and a bag of potatoes, and he wrote a line in pencil without looking up. On the first of the month somebody came in and paid down the page, whatever they could manage that week. Nobody ever asked to see the book, and he never once mentioned a number out loud. If a family was having a bad winter, the page just stayed open a little longer. It was the most honest bank in town, and it ran on a pencil.
posts.first: Our grocer wore a paper hat and kept the pencil behind his ear even when he was off the clock. My mother always paid on Friday, and he always handed her a peppermint stick for me. I did not know until I was grown that the peppermint was free.

posts.quote: THE UMBRELLA STAND HELD ONE UMBRELLA, TWO CANES, AND A BASEBALL BAT NOBODY HAD EVER USED.
posts.caption: Every front hall had a tall stand by the door, and nobody ever sorted what went into it. Ours held one black umbrella with a bent rib, two canes from two different great-uncles, and a baseball bat that had never touched a ball. The umbrella came out only when it rained hard enough that Dad gave up arguing with the sky. The canes stayed in case anybody ever needed them. The bat, as far as we could tell, was there for reassurance. Just knowing it was there made the house feel looked after.
posts.first: My grandmother's stand was an old milk can with a dent in the side. It held a cane that belonged to her father, which no one used and no one moved. After she passed, it stood by the door for another year.

posts.quote: Holding the door for the next person wasn't a lesson in manners class. It was just what you did.
posts.first: My father held the door at the post office for a stranger every Saturday, even on his way out. He called it a minute of his time, and he never missed one. I catch myself doing it without thinking.

posts.quote: THE PICNIC / A CHECKERED CLOTH, A THERMOS OF LEMONADE, AND A SPOT BY THE RIVER
posts.caption: Mom spread the checkered cloth on the grass by the river, and the ants arrived before the sandwiches did. There was a thermos of lemonade sweating through its cork, a wax paper bundle of fried chicken, and deviled eggs packed in a tin so they would not slide. Dad took his shoes off, which was how you knew it was a serious picnic. The kids waded in the shallows while the grownups watched from the blanket, and nobody checked the time. When the sun dropped, we packed the cloth, shook the crumbs out for the birds, and drove home with the windows down.
posts.first: We had a picnic spot on a bend in the river that nobody else seemed to know about. My mother kept the same cloth for twenty years, and it still had a faded stain from a spilled cherry punch. I would know that cloth anywhere.

posts.quote: THE FIRST COLD MORNING, THE RADIATOR CLANKED AWAKE, AND THE WHOLE HOUSE SMELLED LIKE BURNING DUST.
posts.caption: Some morning in late October the radiator under the window would start to knock. It banged and hissed like somebody was inside with a wrench, and the whole house filled with the smell of burning dust. Nobody opened a window, because that smell meant the heat had finally come on. You stood in your pajamas with your back against the warm iron and your toes curled on the cold floor. The cat had already claimed the spot on top. For the next six months that radiator would dry your mittens, your socks, and the occasional wet dog.
posts.first: The radiator in our hallway was painted silver, and it had a little pan of water on top for the dry air. My father bled it every fall with a tiny key he kept on his ring. I can still hear that first hiss, and I remember the dust smell right after.
